summary: South Carolina requires nothing of a seller's alarms at closing; the state's smoke detector statute covers apartment units, and smoke and CO alarms otherwise come in through the building code when a house is built or permitted work is done.
alarmType: The statute that does apply, to apartment house dwelling units with no fire protection system, calls for an approved listed smoke detector installed per the manufacturer's instructions, ceiling- or wall-mounted centrally in the corridor or area serving each group of sleeping rooms, on every story including cellars and basements but not uninhabitable attics, connected to a sounding device or another detector so the alarm is audible in the sleeping areas, and meeting NFPA 72A and NFPA 74. For one- and two-family houses, alarm requirements come from the International Residential Code as adopted statewide by the South Carolina Building Codes Council, which applies to new construction and permitted work, not to a sale.
coAlarms: No CO alarm requirement tied to a sale, and none in the state smoke detector statute. The State Fire Marshal's regulations require a CO alarm outside each separate sleeping area only in a narrow case: foster homes with fuel-fired appliances or an attached garage (S.C. Code Ann. Regs. 71-8301). Otherwise CO alarms come through the building code for new construction.
citation: S.C. Code s. 23-9-155 (smoke detectors in apartment houses); S.C. Code s. 23-9-20 (State Fire Marshal duties, which exclude egress enforcement for one- and two-family dwellings); S.C. Code ss. 6-9-40 to 6-9-60 (statewide adoption of the building codes); S.C. Code ch. 27-50 (residential property condition disclosure, which does not mention alarms)
lastAmended: S.C. Code s. 23-9-155 last amended 1993 (1993 Act No. 181, s. 351)
notVerified: No South Carolina requirement to install, inspect or certify alarms at sale or transfer was found; this is an absence of a rule.
The statute's NFPA references (72A and 74) are to standards long since folded into NFPA 72; which current edition the State Fire Marshal treats as controlling was not verified.
Which edition of the International Residential Code is currently in force statewide, and what its R314 and R315 requirements say for new one- and two-family homes, were not read.
The South Carolina Real Estate Commission's property condition disclosure form was not read; the enabling chapter, S.C. Code ch. 27-50, does not mention smoke or CO alarms.

Local ordinances were not checked. South Carolina's code chapter lets municipalities and counties adopt the latest editions of certain national codes, including property maintenance and existing building codes.
